corpus_definition: How I personally feel about a topic.
usage_note: In my opinion, + clause. Usually at the start of the sentence, with a comma. You can change the person: in her opinion, in our opinion. Don't say 'according to me'.

relations.note: Easy and very common in speaking; in my opinion sounds a little more careful.
Same meaning; a little more formal, common in essays.
Shows it is only your own idea: 'Personally, I prefer tea.'

context.text: In my opinion, Samarkand is the most beautiful city in Uzbekistan. My friend Dilnoza does not agree; she thinks Bukhara is better.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; no forms. Learner trap 'according to me' mentioned in usage note.

corpus_definition: Early enough for a planned event or task.
usage_note: in time + for + noun ('in time for dinner'); in time + to + verb ('in time to catch the bus'). Don't confuse with 'on time' = at the exact planned time.

relations.note: Early means before the usual time; in time means not too late for something.
On time means exactly at the planned time, not late and not early.
Formal: arriving at the exact planned time.
Late means after the planned time, so you miss the start.

context.text: We left home early and got to the station in time for the eight o'clock train. If we hurry, we will be home in time to watch the match.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; the 'on time' vs 'in time' trap is explained in the usage note.

corpus_definition: Money that a person receives from work or business.

forms.definition: money that you get from work, business or other places
forms.example: Her main income comes from her salary at the bank.
forms.note: Common phrases: a high/low income, monthly income, income tax.

syn.note: Very close: money you get from working.
Easy word: money you get from your job only.
Money from a job, usually paid every month; income can also come from business or rent.
Money from a job, often paid every week or hour.
Formal: income of a company or a government.

ant.note: Expenditure is money that goes out; income is money that comes in.
Easier word for the money you use to buy things.

forms.note: There is no verb from this word. Use earn: 'She earns a good income.'
Incoming (arriving, for example incoming calls) is made from come in, not from income.

context.text: My uncle has a small shop in Namangan, and it gives him a good income. His wife also has an income from teaching, so together they save money every month.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (B1). in- is not a prefix here (in + come), so no affix is claimed; incoming is not_family.

corpus_definition: The state of being free and not ruled by others.

forms.definition: freedom from being ruled or controlled by another country
forms.example: Uzbekistan declared its independence on 31 August 1991.
forms.note: Also used for people: not needing help from others ('Young people want independence').

syn.note: Easy word; freedom is wider and can mean many kinds of being free.
Formal: a country's full power to rule itself.
Formal: the right of a region or group to control its own matters.
Related: when people of a place make their own laws.

ant.note: Dependence means needing another country or person to help or control you.

forms.note: There is no verb. Use gain or win: 'The country gained independence.'

forms.definition: free and not ruled or controlled by another country
forms.example: Uzbekistan has been an independent country since 1991.
forms.note: Also used for people who do things without help.

syn.note: Easy word with a wider meaning.
Formal: having full power to rule itself.
Formal: often used for a region inside a country, like Karakalpakstan.
Making its own laws and decisions.

ant.note: Needing help or control from someone else.

forms.definition: without being controlled or helped by others
forms.example: After 1991 the country began to make its own laws independently.

syn.note: Formal and close in meaning.
Related: apart from others, not together.
Easy word: without other people.

context.text: Uzbekistan became an independent country in 1991. Every year on the first of September, people celebrate Independence Day with concerts and fireworks.

reviewer_note: in- + dependence is a real opposite split; dependence/dependent are antonyms, not forms. No -ent/-ence claimed because 'independ' is not a word.

corpus_definition: a very young baby or child in the first year of life

forms.definition: a very young baby, especially in its first year
forms.example: The infant slept quietly in her mother's arms.
forms.note: More formal than baby; common in hospitals and on food labels (infant milk).

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
A baby that was born only a few days or weeks ago.
A child can be any age up to about 12 or more.
An older baby who is learning to walk, about 1 to 3 years old.

forms.definition: the time in your life when you are a very young baby
forms.example: Many children in the past died in infancy.
forms.note: Also means the early stage of something: 'The internet was still in its infancy.'

syn.note: Same meaning; less common.
The whole time when you are a child, not only the first year.

ant.note: The time of life when you are a grown person.

forms.definition: silly and behaving like a small child
forms.example: Stop that infantile behaviour; you are twenty years old!
forms.note: Mostly used to criticize adults who act like small children, not about real babies.

context.text: My sister had a baby in March. Doctors at the clinic in Bukhara check every infant each month, because infancy is a very important time for growth.

reviewer_note: Person noun headword stays in its own noun slot (rule 6); infancy as extra noun. No affix claimed (-cy not in table).

corpus_definition: Suitable for relaxed or friendly social situations.

forms.definition: a relaxed and friendly style or way of behaving
forms.example: I like the informality of small family cafés.

syn.note: A relaxed style, often about clothes or manners.
Related: feeling relaxed and comfortable.

ant.note: Following strict, official rules of behaviour.

forms.note: There is no verb from this word.

forms.definition: relaxed and friendly, not official or serious
forms.example: The party will be quite informal, so you can wear jeans.
forms.note: Also used for language: informal English is what you use with friends.

syn.note: Very close; often about clothes: casual clothes.
Easy word: calm and not strict.
Related: kind and nice to people.
Not done by people in authority or by the rules.

ant.note: Serious and following official rules, like a wedding or a business meeting.
Done by people in authority, following the rules.

forms.definition: in a relaxed and friendly way, not officially
forms.example: We chatted informally with the teacher after the lesson.

syn.note: Very close: in a relaxed way.
Not in an official way.

ant.note: In a way that follows the rules of people in authority.

context.text: The meeting at the café was informal, so nobody wore a suit. We talked informally about our plans, and everyone enjoyed the informality.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (B1). The headword is itself the opposite of formal, so formal/formally/formality appear only as antonyms.

corpus_definition: One of the food items needed to make a dish.

forms.definition: one of the foods you mix together to make a dish
forms.example: Rice, carrots and meat are the main ingredients of plov.
forms.note: Also used for ideas: 'Hard work is a key ingredient of success.'

syn.note: More formal; also used for parts of machines.
Related: one part of something bigger.
Easy general word for a piece of a whole.

context.text: Plov needs only a few ingredients: rice, carrots, onions and meat. My grandmother buys every ingredient fresh at the bazaar in the morning.

reviewer_note: No family forms in any slot; -ent is not claimed because 'ingredi' is not a word.

corpus_definition: To cause physical harm to a person or animal.

forms.definition: physical harm done to the body of a person or animal
forms.example: He had a bad knee injury after the accident.

syn.note: Usually a cut or hole in the skin, for example from a knife.
Related: damage of any kind, not only to the body.
Used for things more than for people.

forms.definition: to hurt the body of a person or animal
forms.example: Did you injure your leg during the game?
forms.note: Often passive: 'Two people were injured in the accident.' For things, use damage.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Usually with a weapon, like a knife or gun.
A wider word: can also be about health or feelings.
Used for things, not usually for people.

ant.note: To make a hurt part of the body healthy again.

forms.definition: physically hurt, for example in an accident or a fight
forms.example: The injured woman was taken to hospital.

syn.note: Easy everyday word.
Usually hurt by a weapon, often in a war.

ant.note: Not hurt at all; a little more common in news stories.

context.text: Aziz injured his knee while playing football in Samarkand. The injury was not serious, but the injured player had to rest for two weeks.

reviewer_note: uninjured goes in ant (rule 3), not as a form. No affix claimed: 'injur' is not a word.

corpus_definition: A quick note sent to someone on the web right now.
usage_note: send someone an instant message; often shortened to IM. Also used as a verb in informal English: 'She instant messaged me.'

relations.note: Sent by phone network (SMS); an instant message is sent through an app or website.
Easy general word for any written or spoken note.
A conversation made of many quick messages.
Also sent online, but usually longer and slower to get an answer.

context.text: My cousin in Moscow sends me an instant message every evening. Instant messages are faster than emails, so we use them for quick questions.

corpus_definition: Information about how to do or use something.

forms.definition: information that tells you how to do or use something
forms.example: Read the instructions before you use the new washing machine.
forms.note: Usually plural: instructions. In formal English it can also mean teaching: 'instruction in English'.

syn.note: Usually plural too: 'Follow the directions on the box.'
Related: advice about how to do something, often official.
Related: help and advice, not always step by step.

forms.definition: to tell someone what to do, often in an official way
forms.example: The teacher instructed us to write our names at the top.
forms.note: Also means to teach a skill: 'He instructs new drivers.'

syn.note: Easy everyday word: 'She told us to wait.'
Formal: to give an official order.
Stronger: you must do it.
Related: help someone learn a skill.

forms.definition: giving information about how to do something
forms.example: We watched an instructional video about first aid.

syn.note: Related: helping people learn.
Related: giving useful facts.

forms.definition: giving useful knowledge or teaching you something
forms.example: The trip to the history museum was very instructive.
forms.note: Belongs to instruct = teach, not to step-by-step information.
Instructively exists but is very rare.

people.definition: a person whose job is to teach a practical skill
people.example: My driving instructor in Tashkent was very patient.

context.text: The instructions for my new phone were only in Russian, so my brother instructed me step by step. Later we found an instructional video online.

reviewer_note: instructive is other_meaning (teach sense); instructively is rare, so adverb is no_form with a note.
